subsection: 9. The impact of war on society and economy; case study: women in the workforce during World War I

notes.h: A world war becomes total war
notes.b: By 1914 the great powers expected a short war. Instead it became a long struggle that drew in whole societies, which is why historians call it a total war.
points: It was a world war because it was fought across several continents, and its effects reached civilians and economies as well as armies.

On the Western Front the war became one of attrition (wearing the enemy down), so armies needed millions of men and huge quantities of shells for years. This need, not ideology, is why states took over their economies and why women were needed.
Total war means that whole societies and economies are mobilised: the state directs industry, labour, food and public opinion, and civilians become targets.

Conscription is compulsory military service. France and Germany already had it before 1914, but Britain relied on volunteers until the Military Service Act of January 1916, which conscripted single men aged 18 to 41 and came into force in March 1916.
The Act was extended to married men in May 1916. Conscription took men out of factories and offices, so it created the demand for women's labour.
notes.tip: Dilution and conscription are different things: dilution is putting unskilled workers on skilled jobs, conscription is compulsory military service. Link volunteering and conscription to the labour shortage to earn marks.

notes.h: Total war in Britain: the state takes control
notes.b: The scale and length of the war forced the British government to direct the economy and people's daily lives, far beyond anything seen in earlier wars.
points: The Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), passed in August 1914 and extended repeatedly, gave the government power over property, labour, the press and public behaviour. It allowed censorship of news and restricted pub opening hours.
British Summer Time was introduced in 1916 to save energy and daylight. It came from a separate act, not from DORA.
The government took control of the railways from August 1914 and of all the coal mines by 1917, and it also took over shipping, so that supplies could be coordinated.
New ministries were created: Munitions in 1915, and Labour, Food and Shipping in 1916. Each gave the state direct control of a part of the war effort.
The Shell Crisis of spring 1915 was a shortage of shells for the army. It brought down the Liberal government, which was replaced by a coalition under Asquith in May 1915.
David Lloyd George became Minister of Munitions in 1915 and led the new ministry that took charge of the supply of war material.
notes.tip: If asked why women were recruited, link the Shell Crisis to the new Ministry of Munitions and then to women's recruitment. Do not describe British Summer Time as a DORA measure.

notes.h: Germany's war economy, propaganda, rationing and civilians as targets
notes.b: Germany also put its economy under state direction. Every government had to keep soldiers recruited, civilians fed and morale up, and the war reached civilians directly.
points: In 1914 Germany set up the War Raw Materials Department under Walther Rathenau to control scarce raw materials. The Hindenburg Programme of 1916 aimed to increase munitions production.
The Auxiliary Service Law of December 1916 compelled men aged 17 to 60 into war work. Because it drew male workers into industry, it increased the pressure on women to fill other gaps.
Propaganda was used to recruit soldiers, as in Kitchener's 1914 'Your Country Needs You' poster, to sell war bonds and to encourage civilians to accept shortages.
Governments also censored newspapers and letters, so that bad news and criticism did not damage morale.

Rationing (sharing out scarce food by rule) came at different times. Germany introduced bread rationing from 1915. Britain brought in compulsory rationing of sugar, meat and butter only in 1918, after the submarine campaign cut supplies.
Britain's Corn Production Act of 1917 was passed to raise food output at home, because imports were threatened by the submarine campaign.
Civilians became targets. German warships shelled Scarborough, Hartlepool and Whitby in December 1914, Zeppelin airships raided Britain from 1915 and Gotha bombers attacked in 1917-18.
notes.tip: For a poster or newspaper extract about the home front, identify who issued it and what it wants people to do (recruit, save, accept rationing), then add background such as the Ministry of Munitions.

notes.h: The economic effects of the war
notes.b: Fighting a war of this size cost enormous sums, and paying for it changed the position of whole countries.
points: States paid for the war through borrowing, war loans and printing money rather than taxation alone, so the national debts of the belligerents multiplied.
Britain, once the world's greatest creditor, became a debtor to the USA because it borrowed heavily to pay for the war, which became the leading financial power.

Inflation (a general rise in prices) meant that prices rose faster than wages in most countries and savings lost value. In Germany, where the war was funded mainly by loans and money creation, this laid the ground for later inflation.
Industry converted to war production, and new industries such as chemicals, aircraft and engineering expanded.
Peacetime trade collapsed because factories and ships were busy with the war, so Europe lost export markets to the USA and Japan.
Agriculture lost men and horses to the army, so governments pushed food production, as in the Corn Production Act of 1917.
notes.tip: Organise economic answers by theme (finance and debt, inflation, industry, lost markets) and explain cause and result, not a narrative.

notes.b: Some economies were damaged far more than others, depending on whether they were blockaded or fought over.
points: Germany's blockaded economy suffered severe shortages. After a poor potato harvest the 'Turnip Winter' of 1916-17 forced people to eat turnips in place of potatoes.
Estimates of German civilian deaths linked to the blockade and malnutrition-related causes range from about 400,000 to about 750,000, so it is safest to say hundreds of thousands.
Areas fought over, such as northern France and Belgium, were devastated.
Russia's economy collapsed under the strain of the war, which contributed to revolution.

notes.h: The effects of the war on society
notes.b: The war killed and disabled millions and shook old social patterns, while also strengthening some groups and the state.
points: About 9 to 10 million soldiers died in all. Germany lost about 2 million, France about 1.4 million and Britain about 700,000 to 750,000 (nearly 900,000 with the Empire).
Many survivors were disabled, and there were very many widows and orphans, so families and welfare systems were put under heavy strain.
Class barriers loosened a little because of shared danger in the trenches, the need for national unity and wider state welfare. Soldiers from town and country also met people from other regions.

Trade unions gained strength and government recognition because governments needed their cooperation. British union membership roughly doubled, from about 4 million in 1914 to about 8 million in 1920, though strikes continued over pay and conditions.
The Education Act 1918 (the Fisher Act) raised the school-leaving age to 14.
The influenza pandemic of 1918-19 killed tens of millions worldwide, with estimates ranging from about 17 million to 50 million or more. It struck young adults weakened by the war.
In 1919 demobilisation (releasing soldiers from the army) brought fears of unemployment, strikes and some army mutinies over slow demobilisation.
notes.tip: Do not give a single exact British death toll, because sources give a range. A paragraph on the Fisher Act should mention schooling only.

notes.b: Before the war most women who earned wages were young and unmarried and worked in a narrow range of badly paid jobs. This is the starting point against which any change must be judged.
points: Domestic service was the largest employer of women in Britain, with well over a million servants. Textiles and clothing came next.
Women's pay was about half of men's or less. They were excluded from most skilled trades and professions and from many trade unions, and married women were expected to stay at home.
In France many women worked on family farms and in textile and clothing workshops.
In Germany women worked mainly in agriculture, domestic service and textiles. They were barred from political associations until 1908, which held back their organisation.
The German women's movement was split between middle-class feminists and the SPD women's movement led by Clara Zetkin.
notes.tip: For short paragraphs on women before 1914, give the jobs, the low pay and the exclusion from skilled trades and unions.

notes.h: Case study: the fight for the vote before 1914
notes.b: Women could not vote in national elections in Britain, France or Germany before the war. This matters because the vote later became the clearest measure of what the war changed.
points: The WSPU (Women's Social and Political Union) was founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. Its members were suffragettes, and from 1905 they used militant tactics.
The NUWSS (National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies), led by Millicent Fawcett, were suffragists who campaigned peacefully.
Remember the difference: suffragettes were militant and followed Pankhurst, while suffragists were peaceful and followed Fawcett.
notes.tip: Do not say the suffragettes were militant from 1903. The WSPU began in 1903 but militancy began in 1905.

notes.h: Case study: why women were needed and dilution
notes.b: Once the war began, men left their jobs for the army and women were drawn in to replace them.
points: Men volunteered in huge numbers and then conscription emptied workplaces, so employers faced a labour shortage.
After the Shell Crisis, the new Ministry of Munitions (1915) turned to women to make the shells the army needed.
Skilled men's unions feared that employers would replace them with cheaper workers. Dilution means employing unskilled workers, including women, on tasks done by skilled men.
In the Treasury Agreement of March 1915 the unions accepted dilution for the duration of the war.
The Munitions of War Act of July 1915 backed dilution and banned strikes in munitions work, so the government could keep production going.
notes.tip: Explain why women replaced men by linking conscription and volunteering to the labour shortage, and the Shell Crisis to the Ministry of Munitions. For the Treasury Agreement, state that dilution was accepted for the duration only.

notes.h: Case study: women in Britain's munitions factories
notes.b: Munitions (shells, fuses and explosives) was the largest and best-known area of women's war work, and also one of the most dangerous.
points: Hundreds of thousands of women worked in munitions by 1918, filling shells and fuses and making cordite (an explosive propellant). They worked at places such as Woolwich Arsenal and the national filling factories, and were known as 'munitionettes'.
Women in paid work in Britain rose from about 6 million in 1914 to about 7.3 million in 1918.
Conditions were hard: shifts of 10 to 12 hours, night work and the constant risk of explosion.
At Silvertown in east London a huge explosion in January 1917 killed 73. At the Chilwell national filling factory in Nottinghamshire an explosion in July 1918 killed over 130.
TNT poisoning (toxic jaundice) turned the skin yellow, which is why women munition workers were called 'canary girls'. It caused illness and some deaths.
The government responded with welfare supervisors and canteens, and set up the Health of Munition Workers Committee in 1915, because poor conditions reduced output.
notes.tip: Link TNT to the name 'canary girls', which refers to yellow skin and not to a uniform. For a poster from the Ministry of Munitions, say who issued it and what work it shows.

notes.h: Case study: women in France and Germany
notes.b: Women in France and Germany also took over from men, though their experience differed in important ways.
points: France lost its men to the army early in the war, and the 1914 harvest was brought in largely by women, children and old men. Women ran family farms and businesses for the rest of the war.

From 1915 Albert Thomas, in charge of French munitions, encouraged women into arms factories. By 1918 women were about a quarter of French munitions workers, known as 'munitionnettes', including at Renault's Billancourt works.
Because so many men were at the front, French women also worked as tram conductors, postal workers, clerks and nurses.

In Germany the National Women's Service (Nationaler Frauendienst) was organised in August 1914 by middle-class feminists including Gertrud Bäumer. It organised food distribution and welfare, so it is a key example of women's voluntary war work.
More women worked in metal, chemical and engineering firms, with Krupp and Siemens employing many more women.
The Auxiliary Service Law of December 1916 took more men into war work, so it increased the pressure on women to fill gaps.
In Germany women bore the burden of food shortages, queuing for food, and from 1915 women led food protests and riots in German cities.
notes.tip: Use the spelling 'munitionnettes' for the French women. For documents questions on Germany, remember the National Women's Service and food relief.

notes.h: Case study: offices, transport, farms and nursing
notes.b: Women also entered many jobs outside munitions, which showed how far the war opened work that had been closed to them.
points: Women replaced men in banks, government offices and shops, because these jobs could be learned quickly, and the numbers of women clerks and typists rose greatly in Britain, France and Germany.
Women worked on trams, buses and railways as conductors, ticket collectors and porters, and as postal workers. Some became women police and firefighters.
The Women's Land Army was formed in Britain in 1917, because the submarine campaign had made food a priority. At its peak it had about 16,000 to 23,000 members.
Voluntary Aid Detachments (VADs, founded 1909) supplied nurses and ambulance drivers. Vera Brittain served as a VAD nurse and later wrote Testament of Youth.
Edith Cavell, a British nurse in Brussels, was executed by a German firing squad on 12 October 1915 for helping Allied soldiers escape. Allied propaganda used her as a symbol.
Auxiliary services were created: the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps (1917), the Women's Royal Naval Service (1917) and the Women's Royal Air Force (April 1918).
In these services women worked as clerks, drivers, cooks, mechanics and telephonists, releasing men for the front.

notes.h: Case study: pay and trade union attitudes
notes.b: Women's wartime work did not mean equality, because both pay and union attitudes held it back.
points: Women's pay rose compared with pre-war women's work, especially for former domestic servants, because munitions paid better than service. It stayed below men's for the same work.
Trade unions feared that employers would use women to undercut men's wages and skilled status.
So they agreed to dilution only for the duration of the war, with pre-war practices to be restored afterwards.
notes.tip: Link union fears to the 'duration only' promise and then to the Restoration of Pre-War Practices Act of 1919. Say only that women's pay stayed below men's.

notes.b: The war split the suffrage movement and changed how the public and politicians saw women.
points: In August 1914 Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst suspended the WSPU's militant campaign, and the government released suffragette prisoners.
The Pankhursts backed the war. In July 1915 the WSPU held a 'Right to Serve' march in London, funded by the government (Lloyd George), to demand war work for women.
Sylvia Pankhurst opposed the war and worked among women in London's East End. Emmeline and Christabel formed the Women's Party in 1917.
Contemporary opinion changed: ministers and newspapers praised women's war work.
H. H. Asquith, long an opponent of women's suffrage, declared his support in the Commons in March 1917, citing women's war service.
notes.tip: Do not attribute the Right to Serve march to Sylvia Pankhurst. Emmeline and Christabel backed the war and Sylvia opposed it.

notes.b: The most visible gain from the war years was the vote, though it was won on different terms in each country.
points: The Representation of the People Act of February 1918 gave the vote to men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification, about 8.4 million women.
In December 1918 Constance Markievicz was elected as the first woman to Westminster, but she did not take her seat.
The Equal Franchise Act of 1928 gave women the vote at 21, on the same terms as men, so the wartime Act's age and property limits were removed.
In Germany a decree of 12 November 1918 gave women over 20 the vote and the right to stand.
Women voted in January 1919 and 37 women were elected to the National Assembly. The Weimar constitution made men and women equal in civic rights 'in principle'.
France gave women the vote only in 1944, despite war work equal to or greater than that of British women.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the 1918 Act (women over 30 only, with a property qualification) and the 1928 Act (equal terms at 21). Markievicz was elected but did not take her seat.

notes.h: What changed after 1918: women's return to the home
notes.b: When the fighting ended, men needed their jobs back and women were pressed to leave. Only some legal gains remained.
points: German demobilisation decrees of 1918-19 made women give up jobs to returning soldiers.
Britain's Restoration of Pre-War Practices Act of 1919 reinstated the old trade rules, in line with the promise given to the unions.
Many women were dismissed from munitions because the the demand for shells had ended, and some returned to domestic service, which was still a major employer in the 1920s.
The Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act of 1919 opened some professions and jury service to women in Britain.
However, marriage bars (rules forcing women to leave a job on marrying) remained in many jobs.
notes.tip: On whether women kept their jobs after the war, the expected answer is mostly no: men took back their jobs.

notes.h: Assessment: did the war change women's position?
notes.b: Examiners reward judgement, so each gain should be set against its limit and against how historians and contemporaries saw it.
points: Achievement: war work showed that women could do skilled and heavy jobs and increased their public presence and confidence. It helped win the vote in Britain and Germany and brought some legal gains.
Limit: most war jobs ended in 1918-19 and women's pay remained below men's. Traditional views of women's roles returned, and the British vote was limited to women over 30.
Contemporary view: many people thought women's war work proved their worth as citizens. Others, including many male workers, regarded it as a temporary emergency.
Arthur Marwick (The Deluge, 1965) argued that war was a catalyst of social change, including the status of women.
Gail Braybon (Women Workers in the First World War, 1981) and others argued that change was limited and temporary, and that the vote owed much to pre-war campaigning and political calculation.
Differences between countries: war work and the vote were linked in Britain and Germany, whereas French women gained the vote only in 1944.
notes.tip: Pair each gain with its limit: jobs gained against jobs lost in 1919, pay up against still below men's, the vote won against over-30s only in Britain and refusal in France. Name Marwick and Braybon and state each view in a sentence.

notes.h: Assessment: the wider impact of the war
notes.b: The war enlarged the state and strengthened some groups, but at a very high human and economic cost.
points: Gains and growth: it was the first total war, and it enlarged the state, increased union power and widened welfare, including the Fisher Act's rise in the school-leaving age to 14.
Costs: casualties of about 9 to 10 million soldiers dead, devastation in northern France and Belgium, inflation, mounting debts and lost export markets.
Britain moved from creditor to debtor while the USA became the leading financial power.
notes.tip: Organise a wider answer by theme (state control, finance and inflation, industry, casualties, unions and welfare, women) and explain cause and result.

keyTerms.definition: A war in which whole societies and economies are mobilised and governments control industry, labour, food and propaganda.
Compulsory enlistment of men for military service, which took men out of industry and created demand for women workers.
A war fought across several continents by many states, whose effects reached civilians and economies as well as armies.
The women who made shells, fuses and cordite in British factories in the First World War.
The employment of unskilled or semi-skilled workers, including women, on jobs that formerly needed skilled men.
The British law of August 1914 giving the government wide powers over labour, property, the press and public behaviour.
The government control of food supplies by fixed allowances, introduced in Germany from 1915 and in Britain in 1918.
The British organisation formed in 1917 to place women as farm labourers and so increase food production.
